3.0.0.en: When David became king over the tribe of Judah, his position began to grow stronger, despite clashes between him and the rest of the tribes under the leadership of Abner. These clashes increased over five and a half years, and increased further after Abner made Ishbosheth the son of Saul king over the rest of the tribes for two years. But victory was David's, and his position grew stronger with the passing of the years, while on the contrary the followers of Ishbosheth gradually weakened, for the following reasons:

3.0.1.en: 1- The weakness of Ishbosheth's character compared with Saul his father or Jonathan his brother.

3.0.2.en: 2- The people's love for David and their admiration of him for his personality and his strength in wars, and their knowledge that he was the true king whom God had anointed.

3.0.3.en: 3- David relied on God, while Ishbosheth and Abner depended on material strength. The clashes continued a long time because of Abner's stubbornness; on the other hand, David did not want to attack Ishbosheth and his descendants, because he had promised Saul his father not to cut off his descendants (1 Sam 24:20-22). Abner is a type of Satan, and David is a type of Christ and the children of God. Although the power of the devil seems enormous, represented by the ten tribes, God gives victory to His children and protects them, so their strength increases, while the end of the devil is eternal destruction. David waited seven and a half years until all the tribes submitted to him, preceded by many years since God's anointing in his father's house, yet David grew gradually stronger and greater. So do not be troubled if God's blessing or His answer to your requests is delayed, but hold fast to Him in spiritual striving by refusing sin and carrying out the commandment, for in the end you will receive many blessings and your relationship with God will grow stronger.

3.1.0.en: Polygamy was permitted in the Old Testament because of the immaturity of God's people, but in the New Testament God restored what He had established from the beginning of creation, namely the union of one man with one woman so that they become one flesh (Gen 2:24). David begot six sons from his several marriages during the period of his reign in Hebron, and the inspired text here gives us all their names. The first (the firstborn) was Amnon, who wronged his sister (ch. 13), and his brother Absalom killed him because of it (ch. 13:29), and his mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel, whom David married after Michal was taken from him.

3.2.0.en: Geshur: a city lying east of the Jordan between Hermon and Bashan.

3.2.1.en: The second son is "Chileab," whose name appears as "Daniel" in (1 Chr 3:1), and his mother was Abigail, who was known for wisdom and good conduct in the story of David with Nabal the Carmelite, and it seems that he died in David's lifetime. The third son is "Absalom," who tried to seize the kingdom from his father and fought him, and was killed, and David returned to his kingdom (chs. 15-19). He was the son of the daughter of the king of "Geshur," whom David married to strengthen his friendship with her father. She was a pagan, but perhaps she joined the faith after her marriage to David. Absalom was killed when he attacked his father David and his men (ch. 18:14, 15).

3.3.0.en: The fourth son is "Adonijah," who proclaimed himself king in the last part of his father's life (1 Kgs 1:11), as being the firstborn, since his elder brothers had all died, but his father appointed Solomon to succeed him on the throne. He was the son of Haggith. The fifth son is "Shephatiah the son of Abital," and no further details about him are given in the inspired text.

3.4.0.en: The sixth son is "Ithream by Eglah." No additional details about him are given in the inspired text either. All of these were born to David in Hebron, apart from those who were born to him afterwards in Jerusalem (1 Chr 3:5).

3.5.0.en: "Made himself strong" for: was zealous for.

3.5.1.en: In the battles that broke out between the supporters of the house of Saul and the supporters of the house of David, Abner, the commander of Saul's army and his kinsman, defended his house bravely, trying to establish the kingdom for Ishbosheth the son of Saul.

3.6.0.en: Rizpah the daughter of Aiah: Saul's concubine, who guarded the bodies of her two sons whom the Gibeonites hanged (ch. 21:8-11). Concubine: a female slave whom her master marries.

3.6.1.en: The system of concubines was in force in that era, and Saul had a concubine named "Rizpah," whom Abner tried to add to his concubines to strengthen his position and authority in the kingdom. When Ishbosheth learned of it he was displeased and rebuked Abner, because by this he had wronged Saul his father.

3.7.0.en: A dog's head: the head of a dead dog, worthless.

3.7.1.en: Abner was greatly troubled by Ishbosheth's rebuke, for he considered it contempt for him, as though he were the head of a dead dog, and a false accusation by Ishbosheth that he was a supporter of David by his wronging the house of Saul in taking his concubine. He reminded Ishbosheth of his great deeds toward the house of Saul, from his leading the army in the days of Saul, then his making Ishbosheth king and defending him against David, so how could he demand of him today to return the concubine as if it were a sin and a great fault that Abner had committed. Perhaps Ishbosheth was afraid, when Abner married Saul's concubine, that Abner would set himself up as king, and this fear confirms that he was far from God and so thought evil of people.

3.7.2.en: It is noticed that Ishbosheth could not answer Abner with a single word, because he had become king by the power of Abner and not by the power of God. Whoever depends on people submits to them and they humiliate him, but whoever trusts in God remains strong however much people change.

3.8.0.en: Dan: the new name which the tribe of Dan gave to "Laish" after they took the place, at the farthest northern border of the kingdom of Israel.

3.8.1.en: Beersheba: a city at the extreme south of Palestine, about 45 km south of Hebron.

3.8.2.en: Abner swore with the formula of imprecation common in that era, which means that the Lord should do evils to him if he did not carry out his decision to abandon Ishbosheth and support David, whom the Lord had chosen and anointed king in place of Saul, so that the kingdom would be transferred from the house of Saul and handed to David, to reign over all the tribes of Israel from the farthest north of the land to the farthest south.

3.8.3.en: Abner relied on his own strength in transferring the kingdom to David and forgot that he was merely a man and that God is the One who orders the lives of His children. So God used him and he agreed with David, but before David reigned over the tribes Abner died (v. 27). Power and ordering belong to God and not to weak human beings.

3.8.4.en: God permitted Ishbosheth's rebuke of Abner and Abner's anger at him so that the whole kingdom would be transferred to David. So do not be troubled by the strength of the wicked and their resistance to you, for however long it lasts, God is able to turn it at the right time to your good.

3.9.0.en: Ishbosheth could not answer Abner because of his great fear of him, for he was the power that protected him, especially since Abner had threatened to take the kingdom from him.

3.10.0.en: "Whose is the land?": that is, the land of the tribes is under my authority, so says Abner.

3.10.1.en: "Saying, Make thy league with me": he declares that the people of the tribes said to Abner, "Would that you make a covenant with David so that we may follow him." The truth is that it was Abner who wanted to make a covenant with David to secure David's forgiveness of him and to become a follower and one of his commanders.

3.10.2.en: After Abner's anger at Ishbosheth, he decided to remove him from the kingship and make David king over all the tribes, so he sent to David declaring his readiness to make a covenant with him and to make him king over all the tribes.

3.11.0.en: "See my face": come to meet me.

3.11.1.en: David agreed to what Abner offered him, but he stipulated that Abner should not come to him to conclude the treaty until his first wife Michal was returned to him. Saul had taken her from him and given her as wife to Phalti the son of Laish (1 Sam 25:44).

3.12.0.en: David loved his wife Michal and desired her return as his wife, so he decided to send also to Ishbosheth, because Michal was living with the tribes belonging to Ishbosheth's kingdom, and he asked him to return his former wife Michal to him. This was a wise action by David, so that it would not be said that he had exceeded the authority of King Ishbosheth in this matter.

3.12.1.en: David asked for Michal for the following reasons:

3.12.2.en: 1- Because he loved her and was faithful in taking her back as his wife when the opportunity came to him, and whoever is faithful in his house is the one who deserves to be entrusted with the kingdom (1 Tim 3:5).

3.12.3.en: 2- By returning Michal he announces before the tribes his kinship to Saul, and so draws their hearts to him, especially the tribe of Benjamin, when he reigns over all.

3.12.4.en: 3- It shows that he was not eager for the kingship and leadership, but for the ordering of his house and the doing of justice before everything, for it would have been easy for him to take her back after becoming king by his royal authority.

3.12.5.en: 4- It is a restoration of David's dignity, which makes the tribes respect him.

3.12.6.en: But the first reason is the most important of the reasons, and it may be the only reason.

3.13.0.en: Phaltiel the son of Laish: a man from the village of "Gallim," one of the villages of the tribe of Benjamin, near Gibeah.

3.13.1.en: Ishbosheth heeded David's request so that no dispute with him would arise, for he knew the strength of David and his men, and he brought Michal to send her to him.

3.14.0.en: Bahurim: a village on the road from Jerusalem to the Jordan, near the Mount of Olives.

3.14.1.en: Phaltiel, Michal's husband, was a loving and faithful husband to her, and since he could not disobey the king's command, he went out to escort her, weeping over parting from her, and kept following her steps until Abner rebuked him, ordering him to stop walking after her and return to his house, so Phaltiel obeyed and returned to his house.

3.14.2.en: Trust in the love of God, who restores your rights to you if you have been wronged, however long the time and however late His answer, for He never forgets you, and in the long time you wait He teaches you and makes you grow in knowing Him, so you find the salvation of your soul, as happened with David, who waited a long time until the whole kingdom submitted to him.

3.15.s.en: (4) Abner proclaims David king over all the tribes of Israel

3.15.0.en: "In times past": for a long time until now.

3.15.1.en: Abner, as a wise man, did not want to make a treaty with David without returning to the elders of Israel so that they would share in the decision and it would become a strong decision, so he reminded them of their desire, for a long time until now, that David be king over them. "Now then do it," for since this was your desire, carry it out by setting him up as king over you, for this desire of yours agrees with the divine will in choosing David as savior of his people from the Philistines and from the other enemies. It is understood from this that the tribes desired to make David king over them, but Abner did not respond to their desire because he thought of himself ruling the kingdom through the weak Ishbosheth, until God permitted the problem between him and Ishbosheth, and so he carried out the people's desire and the will of God by making David king.

3.15.2.en: Here Abner's wisdom shines forth. After his example, every ruler or leader ought not to act on his own opinion alone but to share his decisions with his people or those who work with him, and so ensure their support for him in carrying them out and the success of his plans. So pay attention to the opinion of those around you and involve them in your decisions, even if you give up some of them to put them at ease and secure their response, so that they rejoice with you in all that you do.

3.16.0.en: "Spake in the ears of": addressed them or spoke in their presence.

3.16.1.en: After Abner addressed all the tribes, he addressed the tribe of Benjamin in particular, for it was the tribe from which Saul came, to persuade them to accept David, who was of the tribe of Judah, as king, and not to be partisan for the house of Saul. Abner was able to persuade them because he was a Benjamite like them. After Abner gained the support and agreement of all the tribes of Israel, and especially the tribe of Benjamin, he went to Hebron, the seat of David's kingship, to tell him of everyone's agreement to his reigning over them.

3.17.0.en: Abner came to Hebron accompanied by a delegation of twenty men, perhaps representatives of the elders of Israel, to meet David, who welcomed them and celebrated the meeting with them by making a feast for them. It is obvious that during the meeting they informed him of the collective decision of all the tribes.

3.18.0.en: Abner told David that as soon as he left him he would go and call all the heads of the people and their helpers to come to him, to make a covenant with him and declare their acceptance of him as king, so that his reign would be founded on the collective desire of the people and would be carried out in an official manner. David permitted him to leave, and he left in peace.

3.19.0.en: Joab was absent from Hebron because he and his soldiers were fighting some hostile peoples, and he returned with abundant spoil from this war, and the time of his return was after Abner had left David.

3.20.0.en: When Joab returned, one of his men told him of the meeting that had taken place between Abner and King David, and how he had met with a welcome from the king and left after the meeting in peace.

3.21.0.en: Joab was a strong personality and the head of the army, and had familiarity with David because he was his sister's son. When he heard of Abner's meeting with David and his leaving him in peace, he was very angry, because Abner had been hostile to David for many years with Saul and had tried to kill him, then divided the kingdom after Saul and gave the larger part to Ishbosheth the son of Saul. So Joab went in to David and rebuked him severely because he had not killed Abner and had sent him away in peace.

3.22.0.en: "To deceive thee": to flatter you and cajole you with words of praise and deceive you.

3.22.1.en: And he told the king that he should know that he had come to flatter you and deceive you, so as to learn your secrets and capabilities, so that he could return and plan to take the kingdom from you for the sake of Ishbosheth the son of Saul. This shows the wickedness of Joab and his evil opinion of Abner; he is not wise, loving and forgiving like David, for he accused Abner of spying without any right.

3.23.0.en: Well of Sirah: the name of a well about 6 km from Hebron.

3.23.1.en: Joab went out from David angry and sent, without the king's knowledge, men to overtake Abner and lure him to return again to Hebron, on the pretext of agreeing with the king or with Joab on some matters that had not been covered in his first talks with the king. Abner had reached in his journey a place with a well called the well of Sirah when Joab's messengers overtook him.

3.24.0.en: Abner responded in good faith to the request of Joab's messengers and returned to Hebron, and Joab was waiting for him at the gate of the city. He took him aside in the gate, pretending that he wanted to speak with him privately, but he suddenly drew his sword and killed him treacherously, in revenge for his killing of Asahel his brother.

3.24.1.en: Joab had another purpose in killing Abner, which was his fear of his rivalry with him in the future for the command of David's army. This shows us how self-love leads a person to commit terrible evils.

3.24.2.en: It is noticed that Joab killed Abner at the gate of the city of Hebron and not inside it, because Hebron is one of the cities of refuge, and it is not permitted to kill a person in it by way of blood revenge. For Abner had killed Asahel, yet Joab did not take revenge for his brother. Joab's killing of Abner was treachery, for if he wanted to fight him he should have dueled him, and by this treachery he transgressed the Mosaic Law, which says, "Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly" (Deut 27:24). God permitted the death of Abner because he had wronged David much, whether in his pursuit of him in the days of Saul, or his dividing the kingdom and his clashes with David, and so that no one would think that Abner was the one who made David king, for it was God who made him king.

3.25.0.en: As soon as David learned what had happened, he immediately declared his innocence and the innocence of his kingdom from this treacherous killing.

3.26.0.en: "Let it rest on the head of Joab": let him bear the guilt of killing Abner, upon Moab and his sons.

3.26.1.en: One that hath an issue: this is one of the unclean diseases in the Law.

3.26.3.en: David was not content with clearing himself, but cursed Joab and called down upon him and upon his house diseases and evils as recompense for his deed, so that there would always be among his household those sick with various kinds of issues, leprosy and paralysis, and those killed by the enemies, and the poor in constant need of necessary food.

3.26.4.en: David's curse was like a prophecy of the evils that would befall Joab and his descendants as the fruit of his wronging Abner. It is known that the descendants of evildoers often grow up wicked like their fathers, and so suffer the same woes that the fathers suffered, but if the sons reform their conduct, God has mercy on them and removes His wrath from them (Ezek 18:10-18).

3.27.0.en: Thus Joab and his brother Abishai took vengeance for the killing of their brother Asahel by the hand of Abner during the war, but this vengeance was an evil, unjustified act, because Abner had warned Asahel more than once against following him and asked him to keep away from him, so his killing of him was in self-defense and during the war, whereas the killing of Abner was deceit and treachery. This verse makes clear that Abishai took part in deceiving Abner to go with Joab alone, so that Joab could kill him treacherously.

3.28.0.en: "Gird you with sackcloth": put on sackcloth, that is, coarse clothes, as a girdle, which is what is worn on the waist and extends downward, as an expression of great grief, because a person is distressed when this coarse clothing touches his skin.

3.28.1.en: David declared a period of mourning for the killing of Abner, and asked the people to show all signs of grief, which in that era consisted of tearing clothes, wearing sackcloth and striking the face. He also ordered an official funeral to be arranged, and David walked at the front behind the bier, taking part in the funeral procession of Abner. David grieved for Abner because he was killed treacherously, and he had been a commander in fighting and destroying the pagans as God commanded.

3.29.0.en: Abner was buried in Hebron, the capital of David's kingdom, in his honor, and David wept at his grave and the people were moved by him and wept too. This shows the extent of David's forgiveness and his love for those who are hostile to him, especially if they seek peace.

3.29.1.en: It is noticed that David did not remove Joab from the command of the army although he knew that what he had done was a great wrong, because of the strength of Joab's position. It was not wise to punish him at this time lest disturbances occur, but he received his recompense afterwards at the hand of Solomon by the command of David his father. So David is just even to his sister's son Joab, once he had sinned (1 Kgs 2:31).

3.30.0.en: David lamented Abner with a beautiful poem, denouncing the manner in which this warrior and great commander died, an evil trick by which a simple person might die who is lured by cunning.

3.30.1.en: May you appreciate the virtues of the one who is hostile to you or wrongs you, and try to forgive him however great his mistakes, and remember his good deeds and great works after his death. This is true love, which wrongs no one and forgives all offenses.

3.31.1.en: Among what David said in his lament was that Abner's death was like the death of the noble: he was not bound like a criminal sentenced to death, but he fell at treacherous, wicked hands, as thieves kill an innocent person. These words of lament moved the people, and they went back to weeping for Abner.

3.32.0.en: "So do God to me, and more also": I become deserving of severe divine punishment.

3.32.1.en: David's companions tried to make him eat something because he had not taken any food since the beginning of the day, but he refused to taste food until sunset, although the time was still early for sunset, and David called down a curse on himself if he took anything until the sun went down. David's fast was for the following reasons:

3.32.3.en: 2- Rejection of the evil done to Abner by Joab and his brother Abishai.

3.32.4.en: 3- Offering fasting and prayer for the departed, as was done by the people of Jabesh Gilead (1 Sam 31:13).

3.33.0.en: The people saw and heard what David had done because of the death of Abner, the weeping, the lament and the fasting from food, and they were comforted by this conduct of his, and were pleased with the duty of condolence he performed for Abner, for Abner was a great commander in the eyes of all the people.

3.34.0.en: David's actions confirmed to everyone that he had not instigated the killing of Abner, and indeed that he did not know what Joab was plotting to do treacherously to this great man.

3.35.0.en: David's men tried to console him in his deep grief over the killing of Abner, but he told them that Abner deserved all this lament because he was truly a great man, and his fall is considered a grave loss for his people.

3.36.0.en: David spoke with wonderful humility before his servants and counselors, declaring his weakness before the strength of Joab and Abishai, the sons of Zeruiah his sister. They were strong and had no little control and domination in the kingdom, so David asked God to intervene to repay them for their evil and to preserve his kingdom in truth and justice. Solomon later killed Joab, while Jaasiel, one of the sons of Abner, became chief of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 27:21). The killing of Ishbosheth
